senses.gloss:
utsarga
------------------------------------------
The most common meanings of this word are: a general rule; giving gifts; giving up. Its opposite is अपवाद or exception.
However, it is used in a technical sense also with regard to Vedic studies. A Vedic student has to start his studies in the month of Śrāvaṇa (August/ September) and close in the month of पुष्य (January/February). This ceremonial closing, before beginning it again, is called उत्सर्ग or utsarjana.

Utsavamūrti
------------------------------------------
The main image in the Hindu temple is generally made of stone and is fixed permanently to the pedestal. It is called dhruvabera or acalabera (See BERA for more details.). Apart from this, there will be a few more (two to five) icons made of metal. They are movable ones, hence called calaberas or calamūrtis.
The most important of these, which is used for processional purposes, either in a रथ (chariot) or in a śibikā (palanquin), is called उत्सवमूर्ति or utsavabera. Being next in importance, it is usually kept in the sanctum itself, close to the main image and connected with it by a golden thread called sambandhasūtra.
UtsavamūrtiIt may also be kept outside the sanctum in a separate cell called अर्ध-मण्डप or शुकनासी.
This image is an exact replica of the original—except in the case of Śivaliṅgas—and is big enough to permit elaborate decorations with garments and garlands as also ornaments.
It should always be either in the standing posture (sthānaka) or sitting posture (āsīna) but never in the reclining (śayāna) posture even though the ध्रुव-बेर (like रङ्गनाथ images) may be in that posture.
No worship is normally offered to the main image in the temple as long as the उत्सवमूर्ति is out.
The utsavamūrtis of विष्णु (in any aspect) are always accompanied by the images of Śrīdevī and भूदेवी even though these images may not be there in the main sanctum.

utsava
(‘productive of happiness’)
------------------------------------------
In general, the word means a festive occasion, though quite a few fanciful definitions have been offered.
Utsava—festivals and sacred days—gradually replaced the वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् of the olden days.
They are intended to secure the well-being of all creatures, to bring about peace and plenty and to enable people to get their desires fulfilled.
As for the details of the various utsavas or festivals like Gaṇeśacaturthī, जन्माष्टमी and रामनवमी, see under the respective titles.
Utsavas are a special feature of हिन्दु तेम्प्लेस्. They are classified in various ways. The most common classification is as follows:
Nitya—routine festivities conventionally fixed for the whole year, month and day.
Naimittika—festivals or rites connected with occasional events, prescribed to be gone through in special situations like एच्लिप्से, fire in the temple campus, epidemics, damage to icons and so on.
Kāmya—festivals conducted to secure the desires of the devotees.
There are other types of classifications also.
Temple utsavas of a major kind like the ब्रह्मोत्सव generally involve the following procedure:
Aṅkurāropa (sowing of sprouts); dhvajārohaṇa (hoisting of the temple flag to indicate the commencement of the उत्सव); bherīnāda (beating the big drum of the temple); याग and होम (fire-rituals); balipradāna (food-offerings); mahotsava (processions); tīrthasnāna (bathing the deity in the temple tank); puṣpayāga (flower-worship); dhvajāva-rohaṇa (bringing down the flag).
See also HINDU TEMPLES.
